lead: LEX is a lexical analyzer generator. You write rules that pair a regular expression with a C action. LEX turns those rules into a C function, yylex, that reads characters and returns tokens. This removes the hand-work of building a DFA for every scanner. LEX is used in compiler courses and in real tools where a language has many token classes. Flex is a modern compatible version. Two rules decide a match: longest match first, then the earlier rule.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.8 for DFA recognition and Chapter 1.6 for token patterns.

sections.h3: The three sections of a LEX program

blocks.text: A LEX file ends in .l and has three sections separated by %%. The definitions section holds options, name definitions and C declarations. C code inside %{ and %} is copied near the top of lex.yy.c. A name definition looks like DIGIT [0-9]; later you write {DIGIT}+. The rules section is a list of pattern-action pairs. Each pattern is a regular expression; each action is C code inside braces. The user code section holds C functions such as main and yywrap.

LEX supplies variables and functions. yylex() is the scanner function. Calling it returns the next token code or 0 at end of input. yytext is a pointer to the matched lexeme. yyleng is its length as an int. yyin is the input FILE*; yyout is the output FILE*. The default yyin is stdin and default yyout is stdout. A rule with an empty action, such as [ \t\n]+ ;, skips the match because the action does nothing. If no rule matches a character, the default rule ECHO copies that character to yyout. ECHO is useful while testing, but in a finished scanner it can hide a missing rule.

The generated yylex reads characters and runs the longest-match logic. LEX compiles the patterns into a DFA table, so the scanner does not try rules one by one at run time in the simple sense; the table encodes the decision. The rule order still matters when two patterns match the same longest length.

Suppose two rules can match at the current position. LEX takes the one with the longest lexeme. If the lengths are equal, it takes the rule written earlier. This is why a keyword rule should come before a general identifier rule. If if and [a-z]+ are both rules and the input starts with if, both match length 2. The earlier rule wins. If [a-z]+ is earlier, if is an ID and the IF action never runs for that input.

The same logic applies at every position. LEX does not stop at the first rule that can match. It keeps the longest match and then breaks a tie by rule order. A whitespace rule such as [ \t\n]+ ; should be present in a working scanner; otherwise spaces, tabs and newlines hit the default ECHO rule. Remember that yytext points into an internal buffer and is valid only until the next call to yylex. Copy the lexeme if you must keep it.
This scanner prints token names for keywords, identifiers and integers. The keyword rule is before the identifier rule. The whitespace rule has an empty action, so it skips spaces, tabs and newlines.

Run lex scanner.l to produce lex.yy.c, then cc lex.yy.c -o scanner. Flex is a compatible modern version; the same file usually works with small changes. The scanner prints IF for if, ID x for x, and NUM 12 for 12. Parser generation with YACC is covered in Unit 3.

figure.caption: At if, both the if rule and [a-z]+ match two characters (the two upper boxes); the earlier if rule wins the tie and gives IF. Scanning then gives ID for x and NUM for 12, so 3 tokens and 5 lexeme characters.

spec.title: Worked example: input if x 12
spec.aria: A flowchart for input if x 12: at if both the if rule and [a-z]+ match length 2, so the earlier if rule gives IF; then x gives ID length 1 and 12 gives NUM length 2, for 3 tokens and 5 lexeme characters.

examples.question: A LEX scanner has rules in this order: (1) if action IF; (2) [a-z]+ action ID; (3) [0-9]+ action NUM. A whitespace rule [ \t\n]+ ; skips blanks. The input is if x 12. (a) List the tokens and the length of each matched lexeme. (b) Give the number of tokens and the total number of lexeme characters. (c) If rule (2) is moved before rule (1), what token is produced for the first lexeme, and which rule is unused for this input?
steps: At the first character i, rule (1) matches the literal lexeme if with length 2, and rule (2) also matches if with length 2. The longest length is 2, and rule (1) is earlier, so the token is IF with yytext = if and yyleng = 2.
At the next non-blank character x, rule (1) cannot match. Rule (2) matches x with length 1. Rule (3) cannot match. The token is ID with yytext = x and yyleng = 1.
The next non-blank characters are 1 and 2. Rule (3) matches 12 with length 2. The token is NUM with yytext = 12 and yyleng = 2.
The token count is 3. The lexeme lengths are 2, 1 and 2.
The total lexeme length is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 characters.

If rule (2) is moved before rule (1), at the first character both rules still match if with length 2. The earlier rule is now rule (2), so the token is ID with text if. Rule (1), the IF rule, is unused for this input.
examples.answer: There are 3 tokens with lexeme lengths 2, 1 and 2, and 5 total lexeme characters. With the identifier rule first, if becomes ID because both rules match length 2 and the earlier identifier rule wins; the IF rule is unused for this input.
examples.check:
s = "if x 12"
toks = s.split()
lens = [len(t) for t in toks]
print(len(toks))
for n in lens:
    print(n)
print(sum(lens))

traps: LEX chooses the longest match first; only when two matches have equal length does it choose the earlier rule. Do not say the first matching rule always wins.
The default ECHO rule copies unmatched characters to yyout. A missing rule can therefore look like correct output instead of an error.
yytext is a pointer into a buffer that changes on the next yylex call. Copy the string if the token value must be stored.
Put keyword rules before the general identifier rule. Otherwise a keyword of the same length is classified as an identifier.
yywrap returning 1 means end of input; returning 0 means LEX should get another input file. Mixing these up ends scanning too early or never ends.

quiz.q: Name the three sections of a LEX program.
quiz.a: Definitions, rules and user code, separated by %%.

quiz.q: Why is a keyword rule usually placed before an identifier rule such as [a-z]+?
quiz.a: Both can match the same keyword with the same length. LEX uses the earlier rule for equal-length matches, so the keyword rule must come first to produce the keyword token.

quiz.q: Rules are written in this order: [a-z]+ action ID, then if action IF. The input is if. Which token is produced?
quiz.a: ID. Both rules match if with length 2, and the earlier [a-z]+ rule wins.

quiz.q: A scanner has [0-9]+ action NUM first, then [0-9]+[a-z]+ action ALNUM. The input is 12x. Which rule wins and why?
quiz.a: The ALNUM rule wins. At the start, [0-9]+ matches 12 with length 2, while [0-9]+[a-z]+ matches 12x with length 3. Longest match is checked before rule order.

quiz.q: What do yyin and yyout mean in a LEX scanner?
quiz.a: yyin is the input FILE* and yyout is the output FILE*. Their defaults are stdin and stdout.

quiz.q: What does the default rule ECHO do, and why can it hide a bug?
quiz.a: ECHO copies the unmatched character to yyout. A missing or wrong rule then prints text instead of reporting an error, so the scanner may look as if it is working.

quiz.q: If yytext points to the lexeme 12, what is yyleng?
quiz.a: yyleng is 2, the number of characters in the matched lexeme.

quiz.q: Why should a scanner copy yytext before storing a token value in a symbol table?
quiz.a: yytext points into a buffer that LEX reuses on the next call to yylex. Without a copy, the stored pointer can later show a different lexeme.

beyond: Not for the exam. Flex remains widely used for small scanners and for teaching, and the same longest-match discipline appears in hand-written lexers. Modern projects sometimes use reentrant scanners, scanner generators such as re2c, or parser frameworks such as ANTLR. Search for the Flex manual, reentrant scanners, and scanner-generator input files to see production versions of these ideas.
